blocks.text: We’ll treat X-rays systematically, just as you would encounter them in a medical OSCE, clinical examination, or viva. The goal is not merely to identify abnormalities, but to describe an X-ray accurately, interpret the findings, reach a likely diagnosis, and explain your next steps.
We’ll cover general X-ray interpretation first, then apply it to chest X-rays, abdominal X-rays, skeletal X-rays, and common emergency films.
1. Foundations of X-ray interpretation
Image quality, views, orientation, density, systematic reading, reporting, and common OSCE mistakes.
2. Chest X-rays
Normal anatomy, ABCDE approach, consolidation, collapse, effusion, pneumothorax, pulmonary oedema, TB, and cardiac enlargement.
3. Abdominal X-rays
Bowel obstruction, perforation, ileus, foreign bodies, calcifications, and abdominal gas patterns.
4. Musculoskeletal X-rays
Fractures, dislocations, joint spaces, alignment, bone lesions, and the systematic approach to any bone or joint.
5. Other high-yield films
Cervical spine, pelvis, hip, skull, paranasal sinuses, and common paediatric radiographs.
An X-ray is a form of ionising electromagnetic radiation used to produce an image based on how much radiation different tissues absorb.
Dense structures absorb more X-rays and appear whiter. Structures that allow more X-rays to pass through appear darker.

content_groups.group_title: B. The five basic radiographic densities

blocks.text: 1. Metal / contrast material
Very white
Metal implants and many contrast agents are highly radiopaque.
2. Bone / calcium
White
Cortical bone is very white; cancellous bone has a trabecular pattern.
3. Soft tissue / fluid
Grey
Includes the heart, muscles, organs, blood, and most fluid collections. These structures have similar radiographic densities.
4. Fat
Dark grey
Fat is less dense than water or soft tissue and can help outline anatomical structures.
5. Air / gas
Black
Normal lungs and bowel gas are radiolucent. Abnormally located air may indicate pneumothorax or perforation.
Memory aid: Metal → Bone → Soft tissue → Fat → Air.
From most radiopaque (white) to most radiolucent (black), this is the usual order.

Important: radiographic appearance depends on exposure, processing, patient positioning, and the structure being examined. Not every white area represents disease, and not every black area is abnormal.

rows: Alveoli filled with material, often producing an air-space opacity
An area of bone destruction or reduced density
An area of increased bone density
A structure or fragment is out of its normal position
A fragment or bone segment is tilted relative to normal alignment
Disruption of the outer dense layer of bone
New bone formation along the periosteum

blocks.text: **Do not confuse these terms**

items.text: Opacity describes an appearance, not a diagnosis.
Consolidation is a pattern that may occur in pneumonia, but other causes exist.
Fracture means a break in bone continuity; it may be subtle and difficult to see.
Lucency can represent normal anatomy, air, a cyst, or bone destruction depending on the location.

blocks.text: In an OSCE, never jump straight to the diagnosis. First establish what image you have been given and whether it is technically adequate.

blocks.title: State or mentally check the following:

items.text: Patient: Confirm the name or identifier and age where available.
Date: Check when the image was obtained.
Anatomical region: Chest, abdomen, wrist, pelvis, etc.
Projection / view: PA, AP, lateral, oblique, supine or erect.
Side marker: Confirm left (L) or right (R).
Clinical indication: Why was the X-ray requested?
Comparison: Are previous films available?

blocks.text: In a real clinical setting, patient identification and laterality are essential. In an examination, verbalising the view and side demonstrates a disciplined approach.
PA — posteroanterior
The beam passes from the posterior chest to the anterior chest. Usually taken upright.

items.text: Preferred routine projection for an ambulant patient.
The heart is relatively close to the detector.
Cardiac enlargement is assessed more reliably than on an AP film.

blocks.text: AP — anteroposterior
The beam passes from the anterior chest to the posterior chest.

items.text: Common for bedbound, critically ill, and paediatric patients.
The heart may appear magnified.
Poor inspiration and rotation are common limitations.

blocks.text: Lateral view
Provides a second plane and helps localise abnormalities.

items.text: Useful for retrosternal and retrocardiac regions.
Can help identify lower-lobe disease and assess the thoracic spine.

blocks.text: Oblique view
Shows structures at an angle and can reveal abnormalities obscured on standard views.
OSCE viva question: Why might the heart appear enlarged on an AP chest X-ray?

Answer: The heart is farther from the detector and closer to the X-ray source than in a standard PA projection, producing magnification. Therefore, cardiomegaly should not be diagnosed from apparent heart size on an AP film alone.
For a chest X-ray, use RIPE:
R — Rotation
Check whether the medial ends of the clavicles are approximately equidistant from the spinous processes.
Rotation can distort the mediastinum and make one lung appear different from the other.
I — Inspiration

Check the depth of inspiration. On a well-inspired adult PA film, approximately 9–10 posterior ribs may be visible above the diaphragm, though the expected count varies with technique and patient factors.
Poor inspiration crowds the lung markings and can falsely suggest basal opacity or an enlarged heart.
P — Projection
Identify PA versus AP, and whether the film is erect or supine.
Projection affects heart size and the distribution of pleural fluid or air.
E — Exposure
Assess whether the image is adequately penetrated.
On a standard chest film, the thoracic vertebrae should be faintly visible through the cardiac shadow, without excessive loss of lung detail.
Some teaching resources use different wording for the letters in RIPE. The important skill is to assess rotation, inspiration, projection and exposure consistently.
**What if the film is technically poor?**

Do not automatically call an abnormality. State the limitation, decide whether the film remains interpretable, and consider whether repeat imaging or another modality is justified. In emergencies, act on important findings while obtaining further imaging if needed.

subsections.subsection_title: 3. The universal method for reporting X-rays

blocks.text: A strong report follows a predictable order:
Identification and view
What body part, which side, which projection?
Technical adequacy
Is the image suitable for interpretation?
Systematic anatomical review
Examine all relevant structures in a consistent order.
Describe the abnormality
Location, appearance, distribution, size, extent and associated findings.
Impression and action
Give the most likely diagnosis, important alternatives when necessary, and urgent next steps.

blocks.title: Whenever you see an abnormality, ask:

items.text: Where? Which anatomical region, lobe, bone, joint or side?
What? Opacity, lucency, fracture, displacement, calcification or other finding?
How much? Size, number, extent or severity?
What pattern? Focal, diffuse, linear, lobar, multifocal, destructive or sclerotic?
What else? Associated effusion, soft-tissue swelling, collapse, dislocation or other complication?
What does it mean? What diagnosis best explains the complete picture?

blocks.text: For a fracture, specifically describe the bone, anatomical level, fracture pattern, displacement, angulation, joint involvement and any associated dislocation. Include open-fracture status and neurovascular findings from the clinical assessment where relevant.
For a chest opacity, describe its location, distribution, borders, air bronchograms if present, and associated volume loss or pleural abnormalities.

subsections.subsection_title: 4. Chest X-ray: the most important OSCE application

blocks.text: The chest X-ray is one of the highest-yield imaging stations. You should be able to interpret it even when the examiner provides no clinical history.

content_groups.group_title: A. Use ABCDE for the chest

blocks.text: Use ABCDE for the systematic anatomical review. RIPE assesses image quality; ABCDE assesses the structures.
A — Airway

items.text: Is the trachea central?
Is the carina visible?
Are the main bronchi patent where visible?
Is there mediastinal shift?

blocks.text: Key clue: Shift towards a side may occur with volume loss, while shift away may occur with a large space-occupying process, such as tension pneumothorax or a large effusion.
B — Breathing

items.text: Compare both lung fields.
Assess lung markings and symmetry.
Look for consolidation, collapse, nodules, pneumothorax and pleural effusion.
Inspect the apices and lung bases carefully.

blocks.text: C — Circulation

items.text: Assess heart size and contour.
Examine the mediastinum and hila.
Look at the aortic arch and pulmonary vascularity.
Consider pulmonary oedema or vascular congestion.

blocks.text: D — Diaphragm

items.text: Compare the hemidiaphragms; the right is usually higher.
Check both costophrenic angles.
Look for free subdiaphragmatic air.
Assess abnormal elevation or flattening.

blocks.text: E — Everything else

items.text: Ribs, clavicles, scapulae and visible spine.
Soft tissues, including the neck and chest wall.
Lines, tubes, pacemakers and other devices.
Review the entire film, including areas outside the lungs.

blocks.text: Viva tip: Do not stop when you find one abnormality. A patient can have pneumonia and a pleural effusion, or a fracture and a dislocation. Finish the entire search.

content_groups.group_title: B. Recognising common chest X-ray abnormalities

blocks.text: Consolidation
An air-space opacity, sometimes with air bronchograms and obscuration of an adjacent border. Pneumonia is a common cause.
Report: “There is focal air-space opacity in the right lower zone, with air bronchograms, in keeping with consolidation.”
Pleural effusion
Blunting of a costophrenic angle, a meniscus on an upright film, or homogeneous basal opacity. Large effusions may cause contralateral mediastinal shift.
Report: “There is left pleural effusion with blunting of the left costophrenic angle.”
Pneumothorax
A visible visceral pleural line with absent peripheral lung markings beyond it.
Report: “There is a right-sided pneumothorax, with a visible pleural line and absent peripheral lung markings.”
If tension physiology is suspected clinically, this is an emergency; do not delay urgent treatment for imaging.
Lobar collapse
Look for opacity associated with volume loss, fissure displacement, hilar displacement or mediastinal shift towards the affected side.
Report: “There is right upper lobe collapse, with associated volume loss and superior displacement of the minor fissure.”
Pulmonary oedema
Bilateral air-space or interstitial opacities, sometimes with vascular redistribution, septal lines, cardiomegaly or pleural effusions.
Report: “There are bilateral perihilar air-space opacities with vascular congestion, suspicious for pulmonary oedema.”
These are classic patterns, not absolute diagnostic rules. Always integrate the image with the history, examination and clinical stability.

subsections.subsection_title: 5. Skeletal X-rays: how to avoid missing fractures

blocks.text: For any bone or joint X-ray, use ABCS.
A — Alignment
Follow the normal axes of the bones. Look for displacement, angulation, rotation, subluxation or dislocation.
B — Bones
Follow the cortex along the entire length of every visible bone. Look for cortical breaks, fracture lines, lytic lesions, sclerosis and abnormal periosteal reaction.
C — Cartilage / joint spaces
X-rays do not directly show most articular cartilage. Assess joint-space width, congruity, alignment, osteophytes and subchondral changes.
S — Soft tissues
Check for swelling, gas, foreign bodies, abnormal calcification and joint effusion where visible.

blocks.title: When a fracture is present, report:

items.text: Bone and side.
Anatomical location: proximal, middle or distal third; metaphysis, diaphysis or epiphysis; intra-articular or extra-articular.
Pattern: transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted, impacted or avulsion.
Displacement: direction and degree where relevant.
Angulation and shortening, if present.
Associated dislocation, joint involvement and soft-tissue findings.
Any relevant complications or additional fractures.

blocks.text: For children, remember the growth plate and look for buckle (torus), greenstick and Salter–Harris fractures.

Important: A normal initial X-ray does not exclude every fracture. If clinical suspicion remains high—for example, suspected scaphoid fracture—immobilisation and appropriate follow-up imaging or advanced imaging may be needed.

subsections.subsection_title: 6. How to present an X-ray in an OSCE

blocks.text: Here are two model presentations.
“I have been presented with an X-ray of the [anatomical region] of a [patient’s age]-year-old [male/female], performed on [date, if available], for the clinical indication of [indication].
The examination consists of [number and type of views], namely [AP/PA, lateral, oblique, etc.].

**Image quality and technical assessment:** The images are of satisfactory technical quality for interpretation. The anatomical region of interest is adequately included. The patient’s positioning and alignment are appropriate. There is no significant motion artefact, and the exposure and penetration permit assessment of the relevant anatomical structures. [Mention any limitation if present.]
**Systematic review:** I will assess the images systematically, including the alignment, bones, joints, soft tissues and any region-specific anatomical structures.

The bony structures demonstrate normal alignment, preserved cortical outlines and expected trabecular appearance, with no acute fracture, dislocation or focal destructive or sclerotic lesion identified.
The joint spaces are maintained, with no abnormal widening, narrowing or subluxation where applicable.
The surrounding soft tissues demonstrate no significant swelling, abnormal calcification, radiopaque foreign body or soft-tissue gas, where relevant.
The remaining visualised anatomical structures demonstrate no significant abnormality.
**Impression:** Normal radiographic appearance of the [anatomical region], with no acute osseous or other significant abnormality identified.
**Limitations:** The assessment is limited to the structures visualised and the capabilities of plain radiography. If clinically indicated, further imaging may be required.”
**B.** “I have been presented with a chest radiograph of a [patient’s age]-year-old [male/female], performed for [clinical indication].
**1. Views and image quality**

The examination consists of [PA/AP] and [lateral, if available] views. The image is appropriately labelled and correctly oriented. Image quality is satisfactory, with adequate inspiration, appropriate exposure and penetration, and no significant rotation or motion artefact. The entire relevant thorax is included.
**2. Airway and trachea**
The trachea is central, with no significant deviation. The visualised central airways are patent where assessable.
**3. Lungs and lung fields**

Both lungs are adequately expanded and demonstrate normal aeration. The lung fields are clear, with no focal air-space consolidation, collapse, suspicious pulmonary opacity or interstitial abnormality identified. There is no visible pulmonary nodule or mass on the supplied views.
**4. Pleura**
There is no pleural effusion or pneumothorax. The pleural surfaces show no significant thickening on the supplied images.
**5. Hila and pulmonary vasculature**
The hilar structures are not enlarged. The pulmonary vascular markings are within expected limits, with no convincing evidence of pulmonary vascular congestion.
**6. Heart and mediastinum**
The cardiac silhouette is within normal size limits for the projection used. The mediastinal contours are not widened. The aortic contour is unremarkable for the patient’s age and the projection.
**7. Diaphragms and costophrenic angles**

Both hemidiaphragms are normally positioned and clearly outlined. The right hemidiaphragm is normally slightly higher than the left. Both costophrenic angles are sharp. No free subdiaphragmatic gas is identified on the supplied views, if the relevant regions are included.
**8. Bones and soft tissues**

The visualised ribs, clavicles, scapulae, vertebral structures and other included bones show no acute osseous abnormality. The chest wall soft tissues are unremarkable, with no obvious subcutaneous emphysema or radiopaque foreign body.
**9. Additional structures**
The visualised upper abdominal structures show no significant abnormality within the limits of the examination.
**Impression:** No acute cardiopulmonary abnormality identified on this chest radiograph.”

content_groups.group_title: Chest X-ray: technical points you must mention when relevant

rows: Medial clavicular heads approximately equidistant from the spinous processes
Number of visible posterior ribs or overall degree of lung expansion
PA versus AP; AP may magnify the cardiac silhouette
Vertebral bodies should be faintly visible through the heart on a well-penetrated image
Lung apices, lateral lung margins and both costophrenic angles included
Patient identity, side markers and correct left-right orientation

blocks.text: These are technical checks, not a replacement for anatomical reporting
**Example 2: Normal X-ray of the abdomen**
“I have been presented with an abdominal radiograph of a [patient’s age]-year-old [male/female], performed for [clinical indication].

**1. Technical assessment:** The image is appropriately labelled and positioned. The projection is [supine/erect/decubitus], and the exposure is satisfactory. The anatomical coverage is [describe the structures included], with no significant motion artefact.

**2. Bowel gas pattern:** The bowel gas distribution is within expected limits. There is no convincing dilatation of the small or large bowel. No abnormal air-fluid levels are identified on the supplied erect or decubitus views, if performed. There is no obvious evidence of bowel obstruction.

**3. Bowel contents:** The visualised bowel contents and faecal loading are within expected limits for the clinical context. There is no obvious abnormal faecal loading pattern or faecal impaction identified.
**4. Free intraperitoneal gas:** No convincing free intraperitoneal gas is identified on the supplied views. The sensitivity of this assessment depends on the projection and positioning.
**5. Abdominal soft tissues and organ outlines:** The visualised soft-tissue outlines are unremarkable. There is no obvious abnormal organ enlargement where assessable on the radiograph.

**6. Calcifications and urinary tract:** No abnormal radiopaque calculus is identified along the expected renal, ureteric or bladder regions. The kidneys and urinary bladder are assessed only to the extent permitted by the radiograph.
**7. Bones:** The visualised lumbar vertebrae, pelvis, sacrum and included hips show no acute osseous abnormality.

**8. Foreign bodies and other findings:** No unexpected radiopaque foreign body or abnormal calcification is identified. Any visible devices, tubes or lines are assessed for their position if present.
**Impression:** No acute abnormality identified on the supplied abdominal radiograph.

**Limitation:** Plain abdominal radiography has limited sensitivity for many soft-tissue, visceral and urinary tract abnormalities. A normal radiograph does not exclude bowel obstruction, perforation, urinary calculi or other abdominal pathology when clinical suspicion remains high.”

content_groups.group_title: Example 3: Normal X-ray of bones and joints

blocks.text: “I have been presented with radiographs of the [right/left] [named bone or joint], obtained in [AP/lateral/oblique/other] projections.

**1. Technical assessment:** The images are appropriately labelled, with the relevant anatomical region adequately visualised in the available projections. Image quality is satisfactory for assessment.
**2. Alignment:** The bones demonstrate normal anatomical alignment. There is no dislocation, subluxation or significant malalignment.

**3. Bones:** The visualised bones demonstrate preserved cortical continuity, normal mineralisation and an expected trabecular pattern. There is no acute fracture, focal lytic lesion, suspicious sclerosis or other focal osseous abnormality identified.
**4. Joint spaces:** The joint spaces are maintained, with no significant narrowing or widening. The articular surfaces are preserved, with no obvious erosion or osteochondral defect.

**5. Soft tissues:** The surrounding soft tissues demonstrate no significant swelling, abnormal calcification, radiopaque foreign body or soft-tissue gas. No joint effusion is identified where it can be assessed on the supplied views.
**6. Adjacent structures:** The adjacent bones and joints included in the images show no acute abnormality.
**7. Additional findings:** No other significant radiographic abnormality is identified.
**Impression:** Normal radiographic appearance of the [right/left] [anatomical region], with no acute fracture or dislocation identified.”

2. What does a visible air bronchogram suggest?
3. What causes tracheal deviation towards a lesion?
4. What can push the trachea away from a lesion?

subsections.subsection_title: 8. Final checklist before leaving the station

items.text: Identify the patient, body part, side and projection.
Check technical adequacy and limitations.
Use a consistent anatomical search pattern.
Describe abnormalities before naming the diagnosis.
Look for associated findings and complications.
Give a clear impression and appropriate next steps.
Recognise urgent findings and escalate immediately.

blocks.text: One final clinical rule: never allow a normal-looking film to overrule a seriously concerning clinical picture. Some conditions are occult on plain radiography, and additional imaging or urgent treatment may be required.
**What to look for**

items.text: Focal or multifocal air-space opacity.
Lobar or segmental distribution.
Air bronchograms, if present.
Silhouette sign: loss of a normal border where adjacent structures have similar opacity.
Associated pleural effusion or volume loss.
Distribution: upper, middle, lower zone; unilateral or bilateral.

blocks.text: **Full OSCE presentation**

“This is a chest radiograph in the [PA/AP] projection. The image is [adequate/limited by …]. There is a focal air-space opacity in the [right/left] [upper/middle/lower] lung zone, with [air bronchograms, if present]. The remaining lung fields are [describe findings]. I would assess the cardiomediastinal silhouette, pleural spaces and costophrenic angles for associated abnormalities.
The findings are most consistent with pulmonary consolidation, with pneumonia being a likely cause in the appropriate clinical context.”
Important: Consolidation is a radiological pattern, not proof of infection. Consider aspiration, pulmonary oedema, haemorrhage and other causes when clinically appropriate.
**What to look for**

items.text: Blunting of the costophrenic angle.
Homogeneous basal opacity.
Meniscus sign on an upright film.
Loss of the hemidiaphragm outline.
Mediastinal shift away from a very large effusion.
On supine films, diffuse haziness rather than a classic meniscus may occur.

blocks.text: **Full OSCE presentation**

“This is a chest radiograph in the [projection]. There is homogeneous opacity in the [right/left] lower hemithorax with blunting of the corresponding costophrenic angle and [a visible meniscus, if present]. The appearance is consistent with a pleural effusion. I would assess its extent and look for associated consolidation, collapse or mediastinal displacement.
I would correlate with the clinical findings and investigate the cause. Depending on the size, symptoms and clinical context, thoracic ultrasound and diagnostic aspiration may be indicated.”
Do not automatically recommend aspiration for every small effusion. The decision depends on the clinical situation, suspected cause and safety of the procedure.
**What to look for**

items.text: Visceral pleural line.
Absence of peripheral lung markings beyond that line.
Partial or complete lung collapse.
Size and extent of the pneumothorax.
Mediastinal shift or diaphragmatic depression in tension physiology.
On a supine film, a deep sulcus sign may be present.

blocks.text: **Full OSCE presentation**

“This is a chest radiograph demonstrating a [right/left]-sided pneumothorax. There is a visible visceral pleural line with absence of lung markings peripheral to it. The extent of the pneumothorax is [describe, if assessable]. I would assess for mediastinal shift and other signs of tension physiology.
This finding requires urgent clinical assessment. If tension pneumothorax is suspected in an unstable patient, immediate treatment must not be delayed for further imaging.”
Viva distinction: A pneumothorax does not automatically equal a tension pneumothorax. Tension is a clinical emergency determined by the patient's physiological state and supporting findings.
**What to look for**

items.text: Increased opacity in the affected lobe.
Volume loss.
Fissure displacement.
Hilar or mediastinal shift towards the affected side.
Elevated hemidiaphragm.
Crowding of bronchovascular markings.
Compensatory hyperinflation of adjacent lung.

blocks.text: **Full OSCE presentation**

“There is increased opacity involving the [specified lobe], associated with volume loss and [fissure displacement, hilar displacement or other visible signs]. The findings are consistent with lobar collapse.

I would consider an obstructing lesion, mucus plugging or other causes according to the clinical context. Further investigation, potentially including CT chest, may be necessary to determine the underlying cause.”
High-yield distinction: Collapse is associated with volume loss. Consolidation may produce opacity without the same pattern of volume loss.
**What to look for**

items.text: Bilateral perihilar air-space opacities.
Pulmonary vascular redistribution or congestion.
Interstitial markings and Kerley B lines.
Cardiomegaly, especially on an adequate PA film.
Bilateral pleural effusions.
Other signs of fluid overload.

blocks.text: **Full OSCE presentation**

“The chest radiograph demonstrates bilateral pulmonary opacities with [perihilar predominance/interstitial prominence], accompanied by [vascular congestion, cardiomegaly or bilateral pleural effusions, if present]. This pattern is suspicious for pulmonary oedema in the appropriate clinical context.
I would urgently assess the patient's oxygenation, respiratory distress, haemodynamic status and possible cardiac or renal causes.”
pacs.de
**What to look for**

items.text: Enlarged cardiac silhouette.
Cardiothoracic ratio greater than approximately 0.5 on a properly positioned adult PA chest radiograph.
Associated vascular congestion, pulmonary oedema or pleural effusions.

blocks.text: **Full OSCE presentation**

“The cardiac silhouette appears enlarged, with a cardiothoracic ratio exceeding 50% on this [adequate PA] radiograph. The findings suggest cardiomegaly. I would assess for associated pulmonary vascular congestion or oedema and correlate with the clinical examination and echocardiographic findings.”
Trap: Do not use the usual PA cardiothoracic ratio threshold uncritically on an AP or poorly inspired film. Projection and positioning can magnify the heart.

content_groups.group_title: G. Other important chest X-ray abnormalities

rows: Focal rounded opacity; state location, size if measurable, and margins
May require comparison with previous films and CT assessment
Larger focal opacity; describe location, size, margins and associated findings
Requires appropriate investigation for malignancy and other causes
Gas-containing space within a pulmonary opacity or lesion
Consider infection, malignancy and other causes
Consider disseminated infection and other causes
Consider vascular enlargement, lymphadenopathy or a mass
Gas beneath the diaphragm, particularly on an erect film
Suspect pneumoperitoneum; urgent assessment for perforation
Cortical discontinuity or fracture line in a rib
Assess for associated pneumothorax, haemothorax and other injury

blocks.text: For nodules and masses, avoid diagnosing cancer from the X-ray appearance alone. Describe the findings and recommend appropriate follow-up or investigation based on risk and clinical context.

subsections.subsection_title: 10. Skeletal X-rays: presenting fractures and joint abnormalities

blocks.title: For any skeletal X-ray, use ABCS:

items.text: A — Alignment
B — Bones
C — Cartilage and joint spaces
S — Soft tissues

blocks.text: Always check all visible bones and joints, not just the site where the fracture is obvious.

content_groups.group_title: A. How to present any fracture

items.text: Bone and side.
Anatomical location.
Fracture pattern.
Displacement and angulation.
Shortening or rotation, if assessable.
Extension into the joint.
Associated fractures or dislocations.
Soft-tissue abnormalities and important complications.

blocks.text: **Full fracture presentation template**

“These are [AP/lateral/oblique] radiographs of the [right/left] [bone or joint]. There is a fracture involving the [specific anatomical region]. The fracture is [transverse/oblique/spiral/comminuted/other] and is [displaced/undisplaced], with [direction and degree of angulation or displacement where assessable].

There is [no/evidence of] intra-articular extension, and I would assess the adjacent joint for dislocation or subluxation. The surrounding soft tissues demonstrate [findings]. My impression is a [specific fracture description]. I would assess distal neurovascular status clinically and obtain urgent orthopaedic review where indicated.”
Do not describe a fracture as open or closed from the X-ray alone; that requires clinical assessment.

content_groups.group_title: B. Fracture terminology you must use correctly

rows: Fracture line approximately perpendicular to the long axis
Fracture line runs diagonally across the bone
Fracture line follows a twisting course around the bone
Incomplete fracture with disruption of one cortex, common in children
Compression causes cortical buckling, common in children
A fragment is pulled away by a tendon or ligament attachment
Fragments are driven into one another
Fracture extends into the joint surface
Fragments have lost their normal anatomical relationship

blocks.text: **Displacement versus angulation**

items.text: Displacement: Describe how the distal fragment lies relative to the proximal fragment, using a clearly stated reference.
Angulation: Describe the direction of the distal fragment's tilt relative to the proximal segment.
Shortening: State when there is overlap or loss of normal bone length.

blocks.text: Avoid saying merely “the bone is displaced” when you can identify the direction and degree.
**What to look for**

items.text: Loss of normal joint congruity.
Abnormal position of the articulating surfaces.
Associated fractures.
Joint effusion or soft-tissue swelling.
Neurovascular risk based on the joint involved.

blocks.text: **Full OSCE presentation**

“The radiograph demonstrates loss of normal alignment at the [specified] joint, with the [distal or named bone] displaced [direction] relative to the [reference bone]. This is consistent with a [direction/type] dislocation. I would inspect for associated fractures and assess neurovascular status urgently. Prompt reduction by an appropriately trained clinician and post-reduction imaging are indicated according to the clinical situation.”
Name the direction accurately. For example, a posterior elbow dislocation should not be called an anterior dislocation.
**What to look for**

items.text: Joint-space narrowing.
Osteophytes.
Subchondral sclerosis.
Subchondral cysts.
Deformity or altered alignment.

blocks.text: **Full OSCE presentation**

“The radiograph demonstrates joint-space narrowing involving the [specified compartment], with marginal osteophyte formation and subchondral sclerosis. There is [no/present] associated deformity. These findings are consistent with osteoarthritis, predominantly affecting the [compartment or joint].”
State the compartment if it is clear, such as the medial tibiofemoral compartment of the knee.
bionicenter.com.br
**What to look for**

items.text: Bone destruction or lucency.
Cortical irregularity.
Periosteal reaction.
Soft-tissue swelling.
In chronic disease, sclerosis, sequestrum or involucrum.

blocks.text: **Full OSCE presentation**

“There is an abnormal area of bone lucency and cortical irregularity involving the [bone and anatomical region], with [periosteal reaction or other findings]. In the appropriate clinical context, this raises suspicion for osteomyelitis. Early osteomyelitis may not be visible on plain radiographs, so MRI and relevant laboratory and microbiological investigations may be required.”

subsections.subsection_title: 11. Abdominal X-rays: presenting abnormal findings in full

blocks.text: Abdominal radiographs are less useful than CT for many acute abdominal conditions, but they remain important for bowel obstruction, bowel dilatation, selected foreign bodies and specific patterns of abnormal gas.
Start by identifying the projection—supine, erect or decubitus—and whether the diaphragm and relevant abdominal structures are included.
**What to look for**

items.text: Dilated central small-bowel loops.
Valvulae conniventes traversing the full width of the bowel.
Multiple air-fluid levels on an erect or appropriately positioned film.
Relative paucity of distal colonic gas.
Signs suggesting complications, although plain films cannot reliably exclude bowel ischaemia.

blocks.text: **Full OSCE presentation**

“This is an abdominal radiograph in the [supine/erect] projection. There are multiple dilated central small-bowel loops, with visible valvulae conniventes extending across the bowel lumen. There are [multiple air-fluid levels, if demonstrated] and [relative paucity of distal bowel gas, if present].

The findings are suggestive of small-bowel obstruction. I would urgently assess the patient clinically for dehydration, peritonism, strangulation and bowel ischaemia. CT abdomen and pelvis may be required to identify the transition point, underlying cause and complications.”
cambridge.org
**What to look for**

items.text: Dilated colon, usually more peripheral than small-bowel loops.
Haustral markings that do not normally traverse the full bowel diameter.
Marked caecal dilatation where present.
Relative decompression distal to the obstruction.
Associated small-bowel dilatation if the ileocaecal valve is incompetent.

blocks.text: **Full OSCE presentation**

“The abdominal radiograph demonstrates dilatation of the large bowel, predominantly involving the [specified segments], with visible haustral markings. There is [relative distal decompression or other relevant findings]. The appearance is concerning for large-bowel obstruction.
I would assess the patient urgently and arrange further imaging, usually CT where appropriate, to determine the level, cause and presence of complications.”
**What to look for**

items.text: Free gas beneath the diaphragm on an erect chest or abdominal radiograph.
Free gas in the abdomen on appropriate decubitus or supine views.
Rigler sign, in which both sides of the bowel wall become visible, in suitable circumstances.
Other signs of abnormal intraperitoneal gas.

blocks.text: **Full OSCE presentation**

“There is free gas beneath the [right/left] hemidiaphragm, consistent with pneumoperitoneum. In a patient without a recent operation or another recognised explanation, this raises strong concern for hollow-viscus perforation.
I would arrange immediate surgical assessment and resuscitation as clinically indicated. Further imaging must not delay necessary intervention in an unstable patient.”
sdelatmrt.spb.ru
**What to look for**

items.text: Diffuse bowel dilatation involving both small and large bowel.
Gas extending into the colon and rectum.
No convincing discrete transition point on the available film.

blocks.text: **Full OSCE presentation**

“The abdominal radiograph demonstrates diffuse gaseous dilatation of both small and large bowel, with gas extending into the distal bowel. There is no definite focal transition point visible on this examination. The appearance may represent an ileus, although mechanical obstruction cannot be excluded on plain radiography alone.”

rows: “There is a substantial faecal burden within the colon, particularly involving …”
“There is a radiopaque focus projected over the expected course of the … ureter.” Confirm with appropriate imaging if needed.
“There is a radiopaque foreign body projected over …” Describe its number, shape, location and whether serial imaging is needed.
“There is a calcific opacity in the region of …” Consider the anatomical location and differential diagnosis.
“There is marked colonic dilatation in the clinical context of severe colitis.” This requires urgent clinical assessment.

blocks.text: Remember: a plain abdominal X-ray does not reliably exclude appendicitis, bowel ischaemia, perforation or many other serious abdominal conditions.
Skull radiographs have a limited role in many modern head-injury pathways, where CT is preferred when indicated. Nevertheless, the following terminology may appear in OSCEs.
epos.myesr.org
**What to look for**

items.text: Linear lucency that may cross normal skull markings.
Depressed or displaced bone fragments.
Diastasis of sutures.
Associated soft-tissue swelling.

blocks.text: **Full OSCE presentation**

“The skull radiograph demonstrates a linear lucency involving the [specified region], suspicious for a skull fracture. I would assess for displacement and associated injury. In a patient with significant head trauma or neurological symptoms, CT head is the appropriate investigation when indicated.”

When facial bone radiographs are supplied, describe the affected bone, cortical discontinuity, displacement and any associated sinus opacity or fluid level. If an orbital or complex facial fracture is suspected, CT is generally more informative.
Do not mistake normal sutures, vascular grooves or other anatomical variants for fractures.

subsections.subsection_title: 13. Bone lesions: presenting lytic, sclerotic and aggressive abnormalities

blocks.text: These findings are important because the examiner may show you an X-ray without naming the condition.
A lytic lesion appears as an area of increased radiolucency within bone, suggesting reduced bone density or destruction.

items.text: Anatomical location and bone involved.
Whether the lesion is central, eccentric, metaphyseal, diaphyseal or epiphyseal.
Geographic, moth-eaten or permeative pattern.
Zone of transition and margin definition.
Cortical thinning or destruction.
Periosteal reaction and soft-tissue mass.
Pathological fracture, if present.

blocks.text: **Full OSCE presentation**

“There is a lytic lesion involving the [bone and anatomical region]. The lesion is [well-defined/ill-defined] with a [narrow/wide] zone of transition. There is [no/present] cortical destruction, periosteal reaction or associated soft-tissue mass. These features suggest a [less aggressive/aggressive] bone lesion, although the diagnosis cannot be established from this finding alone. Further assessment with appropriate imaging and specialist review is indicated.”

A narrow zone of transition often suggests a slower-growing process; a wide zone, cortical destruction or aggressive periosteal reaction raises concern for an aggressive lesion. These are tendencies, not absolute rules.
A sclerotic lesion appears more radiopaque than the surrounding bone.
**Full OSCE presentation**

“There is a focal area of increased bone density involving the [bone and location]. The lesion is [well-defined/ill-defined] and demonstrates [describe margins, cortical involvement and other features]. This represents a sclerotic bone lesion. The differential diagnosis depends on the patient's age, clinical history, lesion morphology and distribution.”
Potential causes include benign bone islands, healing lesions, selected primary bone tumours and osteoblastic metastases.
Describe the pattern rather than merely saying “periosteal reaction present.”

rows: Often associated with a slower or more organised process
May occur in aggressive or rapidly evolving processes
Periosteum elevated by an underlying process; can occur with aggressive lesions

blocks.text: OSCE caution: No single periosteal pattern establishes a specific tumour. Clinical context, the entire radiographic appearance and further investigations are essential.
Children's bones differ from adults' bones because their growth plates are open and their bones are more flexible.

“The radiograph demonstrates an incomplete fracture of the [bone], with disruption of one cortex and bending of the opposite cortex. The appearance is consistent with a greenstick fracture. I would assess angulation, displacement and the adjacent growth plate.”
“There is cortical buckling involving the [bone and location], without a complete fracture line traversing both cortices. This is consistent with a buckle fracture.”
Always identify the growth plate and look for extension into the metaphysis or epiphysis.
A Salter–Harris type V injury can be radiographically subtle or initially occult.
**Full presentation example: Salter–Harris II**

“There is a fracture involving the distal [bone], extending through the physis into the metaphysis, with a metaphyseal fragment visible. The pattern is consistent with a Salter–Harris type II fracture. I would assess displacement, alignment and joint congruity, and arrange appropriate paediatric orthopaedic management.”
In children, do not overlook the growth plate simply because the fracture line is subtle.

subsections.subsection_title: 14. How to present multiple abnormalities on one X-ray

blocks.text: Sometimes the examiner deliberately gives you a film with more than one finding.

items.text: Identify the most urgent or clinically significant abnormality.
Describe it fully.
Mention other relevant abnormalities.
State the overall impression.
Identify urgent action and additional assessment.

blocks.text: “This is a chest radiograph demonstrating fractures of the right lateral ribs, with an associated right-sided pneumothorax. The pneumothorax is the immediate concern because it may compromise ventilation. I would assess the patient's respiratory status and haemodynamic stability urgently, examine for associated haemothorax and other thoracic injuries, and arrange immediate management according to clinical severity.”

“The radiographs demonstrate a displaced fracture of the [bone] involving the [anatomical region], associated with dislocation of the adjacent joint. I would describe the fracture pattern and displacement, assess joint congruity and look for additional fractures. I would urgently assess neurovascular status and arrange appropriate orthopaedic management.”
Never let a minor incidental finding distract you from a life-threatening abnormality.

subsections.subsection_title: 15. Normal versus abnormal presentation: what changes?

blocks.text: A common OSCE mistake is describing an abnormality without explaining how it differs from normal anatomy.

rows: Focal opacity in the right lower zone
Blunting of the left costophrenic angle consistent with effusion
Enlarged cardiac silhouette on an adequate PA film
Loss of normal joint congruity consistent with dislocation
Multiple dilated small-bowel loops with air-fluid levels

blocks.text: The strongest presentations combine objective description with a justified interpretation.

subsections.subsection_title: 16. Phrases that improve your OSCE performance

blocks.text: Use these phrases to sound precise and clinically safe.
When you are confident
“The findings are consistent with …”
“The radiographic appearance is characteristic of …”
“There is a fracture involving …, with associated …”
When the findings are suggestive but not definitive
“The findings are suspicious for …”
“The appearance raises the possibility of …”
“This pattern may represent …; clinical correlation and further imaging may be required.”
When the image is limited
“Interpretation is limited by poor inspiration and patient rotation.”
“No definite fracture is identified on these views; however, an occult fracture cannot be excluded if clinical suspicion remains high.”
Avoid vague statements such as “the X-ray is bad,” “something is wrong with the lungs,” or “the bone is not normal.” State the actual finding and its location.

subsections.subsection_title: 17. Common examiner questions after you present an abnormal X-ray

rows: What is your most likely diagnosis?
State one leading diagnosis and the findings supporting it.
Give relevant alternatives, not an exhaustive list.
What additional views would you request?
Specify views or imaging that address the suspected injury or abnormality.
What complications are you concerned about?
Name complications specific to the diagnosis.
Discuss stability, urgent treatment, clinical examination and further investigation.
Can you exclude this diagnosis on the X-ray?
Acknowledge limitations and the possibility of occult disease.
Identify physiological threats and the need for immediate escalation.

content_groups.group_title: A model response to “What would you do next?”

blocks.text: For a suspected fracture, you might say:

“I would assess the patient clinically, including distal neurovascular status, check for an open injury and examine for associated injuries. I would provide appropriate analgesia and immobilisation, arrange orthopaedic review and obtain further imaging if required by the fracture pattern.”
For suspected pneumothorax:

“I would immediately assess airway, breathing and circulation, check oxygenation and haemodynamic status, and determine whether tension physiology is present. If tension pneumothorax is suspected in an unstable patient, I would arrange immediate decompression according to emergency protocols without delaying for imaging.”
For suspected bowel obstruction:

“I would assess the patient for dehydration, peritonism and signs of bowel ischaemia, commence appropriate resuscitation and arrange urgent surgical assessment. CT may be required to identify the cause and complications.”
These responses demonstrate that you understand imaging findings as part of clinical management, not as isolated examination facts.
